title: Latency & cost storyboard: mini-benchmark QA memo
content:
Purpose:
This is a compact, storyboard-style QA memo documenting a small set of bench runs we used to validate a pacing change on the slot allocator. The goal: capture human-readable latency/cost tradeoffs across three representative traffic shapes (microburst, conversational-sustained, background-batch) and turn them into a short set of recommendations for follow-up experiments.

Audience:
Platform eng + Observability + Optimize product. Not formal perf report — meant to be readable by on-call and PMs.

Summary (TL;DR):
- Pacing multiplier reduction from 1.0 -> 0.8 reduced average $/query by ~9% for conversational-sustained load with negligible p50 impact but increased p99 by ~12ms in worst-case microburst bursts.
- For microbursts, priority-preempt path still needed: lower pacing alone increases tail amplification when slot contention hits ~85%.
- Recommend: ship 0.8 pacing to low-tier capacity with an automatic circuit that reverts to 1.0 when contention >80% for >30s (short term). Meanwhile implement priority-preempt guard for true microburst flows (mid term).

Bench setup (small footprint, reproducible):
- Hardware: 4x A100-sim nodes (internal lab), identical batch sizes and model shard layout.
- Runtime: branch runtime/pacing-experiments (PR linked above), default kernels.
- Model: open-lm 13B equivalent (decode heavy; KV cache used).
- Workloads (synthetic):
  1) Microburst: 5s spike to 400qps from baseline 60qps; 70% short replies (<=32 tokens).
  2) Conversational-sustained: steady 80qps with 40% long replies (>=256 tokens), mixed session affinity (30% reuse).
  3) Background-batch: queued batched embeddings-style columns: 20 qps but batched into groups (effective throughput high per GPU).
- Metric capture: per-request p50/p90/p99 end-to-end (client-observed) and server token accounting used to estimate $/query via our internal unit costs (GPU-minute amortized + infra egress).

Key raw results (median of 3 runs each):

ASCII table:
Scenario           | pacing | qps   | p50(ms) | p90(ms) | p99(ms) | throughput/qps | $/query (est)
-------------------|--------|-------|---------|---------|---------|----------------|------------
Microburst         | 1.0    | 400→60| 42      | 120     | 420     | 400-peak       | 0.0125
Microburst         | 0.8    | 400→60| 45      | 135     | 472     | 400-peak       | 0.0113
Conversational     | 1.0    | 80    | 60      | 110     | 180     | steady-80      | 0.0180
Conversational     | 0.8    | 80    | 62      | 112     | 202     | steady-80      | 0.0164
Background-batch   | 1.0    | 20    | 120     | 250     | 400     | batched-high   | 0.0076
Background-batch   | 0.8    | 20    | 125     | 260     | 410     | batched-high   | 0.0069

Notes on table: $/query is rough (GPU amort + infra); relative differences are the signal. Microburst $/query declines ~9.6% (1.25c -> 1.13c). Conversational shows ~8.9% reduction.

Visual / ASCII mini-charts (p99 sensitivity):
Microburst p99 (ms): 1.0=[##########] 420ms  | 0.8=[############] 472ms
Conversational p99 (ms): 1.0=[######] 180ms | 0.8=[########] 202ms
Background-batch p99 (ms): 1.0=[#########] 400ms | 0.8=[##########] 410ms

Interpretation / reading the storyboard:
- Why cost drops: lower pacing increases slot packing (more effective occupancy), reduces idle GPU time, so amortized cost per token drops.
- Why tails worsen for microburst: reduced pacing leaves fewer reserve slots for instantaneous spikes resulting in higher queueing/backpressure; the burst amplification especially visible at the tail when multiple sessions collide.
- Conversational workloads tolerate pacing reduction best because session affinity and longer replies allow KV cache reuse and higher packing efficiency. The small p50 bump (~2ms) is within typical noise.
- Background-batch benefits least in p99 but sees nice cost wins due to deterministic batching; the p99 here is dominated by batch skew rather than pacing.

Quick QA notes (things to validate before wider rollout):
- Re-run microburst with higher variance spike shapes (3s, 7s, 12s) to ensure tail behavior is consistent.
- Test with two model sizes (7B and 70B quantized path) — packing dynamics differ.
- Confirm that the $/query delta remains for larger cluster sizes and multi-tenant scheduling (we used single-tenant lab nodes).
- Validate metrics instrumentation: ensure client-observed p99 lines up with server-side queuing traces (Trace IDs in linked PR).

Actionable recommendations (short):
1) Pilot: flip pacing to 0.8 on a low-priority capacity pool (non-critical customers) for 48h with increased tail monitoring alarms (p99 + eviction rates).
2) Guard: implement auto-revert when slot contention >80% for longer than 30s.
3) Microburst mitigation: pair pacing reduction with a lightweight priority-preempt path (fastpath) so critical microburst sessions can preempt a small percentage of slots.
4) Experiment: run targeted bench matrix next week scaling to 8 nodes and adding multi-tenant noise. Keep the storyboard notes and compare to these runs.

Appendix A — quick-run checklist for reproducibility:
- Checkout: runtime/pacing-experiments @PR-3189
- Command scripts: bench/microburst/bench.sh --seed 2026 --shape microburst --pacing {1.0,0.8}
- Dashboard filters: filter by trace-tag=pacing-exp and add column: server.slot-contention, client.p99
- Observability: look at slot eviction histogram and admission_reject_rate per 10s bucket.

Appendix B — open questions / unresolved:
- Is 0.8 the global sweet spot across all customer mixes? Probably not — needs multi-tenant sweep.
- How should we allocate priority budget across capacity classes? Ops input required.
- Does quantized 70B change tail curvature? Early signal: more sensitive due to longer per-token kernel times.

Contact: Lucas Chen (platform eng) — ping in #plat-bench if you want the raw CSVs.

End of memo.
